essays.title: The Six Strategic Goals: How the Bosnian Serb Assembly Chose War
essays.content:
On 12 May 1992, the Assembly of the Republika Srpska convened in Banja Luka to formalize the war aims that would drive Bosnian Serb military and political strategy for the next three and a half years. With Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence referendum having passed on 1 March and international recognition following on 6 April, the Bosnian Serb leadership under Radovan Karadžić moved to codify a territorial vision that rejected the new state's legitimacy. The session produced what became known as the Six Strategic Goals of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

The six goals, as presented by Karadžić and adopted by the assembly, were explicit in their scope. The first called for the separation of Serb peoples from the other two constituent nations — Bosniaks and Croats. The second demanded the establishment of a corridor through the Posavina region in northern Bosnia, linking Serb-held territories in the west with Serbia proper. The third sought control of the Drina River valley, creating a contiguous border with Serbia along Bosnia's eastern frontier. The fourth aimed to establish the Una and Neretva rivers as natural borders of the Serb entity. The fifth called for the partition of Sarajevo into separate Serb and Bosniak zones. The sixth asserted Bosnian Serb access to the Adriatic Sea. Taken together, these objectives constituted a comprehensive program for redrawing Bosnia's internal geography along ethnic lines, implying the displacement of non-Serb populations from enormous swathes of territory.

The ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) established that these goals were central to the joint criminal enterprise through which crimes against non-Serb civilians were organized and carried out across Bosnia. The judgment found that the strategic objectives, declared openly in a legislative chamber, provided the framework within which subsequent military campaigns, forced population transfers, and acts of persecution were planned and executed. The ICJ in its 2007 Bosnia v. Serbia judgment similarly treated the political declarations of this period as relevant context for its analysis of subsequent events and their legal character.

Also present at the session was General Ratko Mladić, newly appointed commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. Mladić addressed the assembly in terms that would later feature prominently in ICTY proceedings. He spoke with a bluntness that contrasted sharply with the political language of the assembly’s resolutions, warning that the military campaigns necessary to achieve the stated goals would be prolonged and devastating. His remarks were later cited in ICTY proceedings as evidence that the Bosnian Serb leadership understood, from the outset, the scale of violence their territorial program would require.

From the Bosnian Serb perspective, the goals represented the protection of a community that feared minority status within an independent, Bosniak-majority state. From the perspective of Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats, the same framework constituted an existential threat — a blueprint for ethnic cleansing dressed in the language of national self-determination. The significance of 12 May 1992 lies in its documentary clarity. The Six Strategic Goals were not inferred after the fact by prosecutors or historians; they were proclaimed openly, recorded officially, and pursued systematically. They remain among the most important documents for understanding why the Bosnian War unfolded with such geographic scope and demographic ferocity across so many fronts simultaneously.

essays.title: Civic Republic or National State: The Bosnian Identity Dilemma
essays.content:
When Bosnia-Herzegovina moved toward independence in the spring of 1992 — with a referendum on 1 March and international recognition on 6 April — its government inherited a profound and unresolved question: what kind of state would Bosnia actually be? This was not an abstract philosophical problem. It sat at the heart of the political crisis that consumed the country for the next three years, shaping military strategies, diplomatic positions, and the daily lives of millions of citizens.

Bosnia-Herzegovina had long existed as a territory where Bosniak Muslims, Orthodox Serbs, and Catholic Croats lived in close proximity, often intermingled across the same towns and villages. The republic's communist-era identity had deliberately emphasized a shared Yugoslav civic character, subordinating ethnicity to socialist brotherhood. When Yugoslavia began to dissolve, this equilibrium collapsed rapidly. Political parties organized overwhelmingly along ethnic lines following the 1990 elections, and the question of whether Bosnia would be a civic, multiethnic republic or a collection of ethnically defined territories became the defining political fault line.

The government of President Alija Izetbegović and his Party of Democratic Action (Stranka demokratske akcije, SDA) championed the vision of a unified, civic Bosnian state in which citizenship rather than ethnicity would determine political rights. This position drew support from Bosniak political leadership and from significant numbers of urban Bosnians of all backgrounds who identified with the republic rather than with any single national group. The Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina reflected this aspiration in its early composition. Established by presidential decree on 15 April 1992, the ARBiH was organized into a corps structure through mid-1992 and included soldiers of Bosniak, Serb, Croat, and other backgrounds — representing at least a formal commitment to multiethnic defense of a multiethnic state. As the war intensified and ethnic violence escalated, maintaining that diverse composition became increasingly difficult, and the army's character gradually shifted toward a predominantly Bosniak force.

The Bosnian Serb leadership, organized through the Serbian Democratic Party (Srpska demokratska stranka, SDS) under Radovan Karadžić, rejected this civic framework categorically. As established in the ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), the Bosnian Serb leadership pursued the creation of a territorially contiguous Serb-dominated entity, arguing that Serbs could not remain as a minority within a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. The judgment details how this political objective translated directly into the planning and execution of territorial campaigns, making the identity question inseparable from the violence that followed.

Bosnian Croat political leadership, centered in the Croatian Democratic Union (Hrvatska demokratska zajednica, HDZ) and closely linked to Zagreb, pursued its own vision of Croat self-determination within or alongside Bosnia, further complicating any prospect of a unified civic settlement.

The consequences of this unresolved dilemma were catastrophic. Because no consensus existed on the fundamental nature of the state, political disagreements found no constitutional outlet and instead became military contests over territory. Cities like Sarajevo, Mostar, and Banja Luka became symbols of competing visions of belonging. The 1995 Dayton Agreement ended the fighting but embedded the tension into Bosnia's postwar constitutional structure, creating a state whose institutional architecture reflected the wartime ethnic divisions even as it formally preserved a single sovereign entity. Whether this arrangement represented pragmatic peacemaking or the codification of wartime gains remains one of the most debated questions in Balkan politics to this day.

essays.title: Herceg-Bosna: Zagreb's Project and the Croat Dilemma
sources: ICTY Prlic et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T), JCE findings
essays.content:
As the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia collapsed in 1991, its constituent communities faced urgent and painful questions about security, identity, and political survival. For the Croat population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, these questions produced a fateful answer: the creation of a parallel Croat political structure that would define — and ultimately complicate — their role in the coming war.

The foundations were laid in late 1991, when Croatian President Franjo Tuđman met with Mate Boban, a senior Bosnian Croat political figure who would later become president of Herceg-Bosna in 1992, in Zagreb. This meeting signaled Zagreb’s direct involvement in shaping the political destiny of Bosnian Croats. Tuđman’s government viewed western Herzegovina and parts of central Bosnia as strategically and culturally significant. As documented in the ICTY Prlić et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T), Tuđman’s preferred outcome was the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina between Croatia and Serbia — a vision the tribunal found he discussed with Serbian President Milošević. The Zagreb meeting established a relationship of patronage and direction between the Croatian state and Bosnian Croat political leadership that would prove consequential throughout the war.

In November 1991, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had been proclaimed in Grude. Boban would assume its presidency the following year. By 1992, as Bosnia-Herzegovina declared independence and Serbian military forces launched devastating offensives against Bosnian cities and towns, Herceg-Bosna’s leaders moved to consolidate autonomous administrative, military, and territorial control. The Croatian Defence Council, known by its acronym HVO, became the armed expression of this project.

The ICTY Kordić Trial Judgment (IT-95-14/2-T) established how Herceg-Bosna functioned as a political and military structure with ambitions extending well beyond local self-defense, documenting the organized character of the HVO and its relationship to broader Croatian political objectives. The ICTY Prlić et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T) went further, identifying through its Joint Criminal Enterprise findings a coordinated effort among Bosnian Croat and Croatian political and military leaders to establish Croat dominance over claimed territories, including areas with mixed or Bosniak-majority populations. The tribunal found that this enterprise operated with the knowledge and support of the Croatian state at the highest levels.

The dilemma facing ordinary Bosnian Croats was genuine and should not be dismissed. Living as a minority within a state under siege, many feared absorption into a Serb-dominated rump Yugoslavia or marginalization within a Bosniak-majority government. Early cooperation between Croat and Bosniak forces against Serbian aggression — particularly in the Posavina corridor and around Mostar — illustrated that unified resistance was possible and could be effective. Yet the parallel ambitions embedded in the Herceg-Bosna project created structural tensions that fractured this alliance by 1993, when Croat and Bosniak forces turned against each other in devastating internecine conflict, particularly in central Bosnia and the Neretva valley.

For strategic understanding, Herceg-Bosna represents a case study in how wartime conditions enable political projects that might otherwise lack legitimacy or momentum. External sponsorship from Zagreb, weak central Bosnian state authority, and the chaos of multifront conflict created space for a para-state to establish itself. The consequences shaped the entire trajectory of the war, dividing the anti-Serb coalition at critical moments and introducing a third axis of conflict that prolonged civilian suffering across Bosnia-Herzegovina.

essays.title: The Arms Embargo: How the UN Disarmed Bosnia's Defenders
essays.content:
When the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia began fracturing along ethnic and political lines in 1991, the international community moved quickly to contain the spreading violence. On 25 September 1991, the United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 713, imposing a comprehensive arms embargo on all territories of the former Yugoslavia. The resolution was intended as a neutral, conflict-limiting measure. In practice, its consequences fell with striking unevenness upon the parties who would soon be fighting for control of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

The strategic logic behind Resolution 713 appeared sound at the time of its passage. Fighting had already erupted in Croatia, and diplomats hoped that restricting weapons supplies would prevent further escalation. What the resolution could not account for was the vastly different military starting positions of the parties involved. The Yugoslav People’s Army, known by its acronym JNA, was one of the larger standing militaries in socialist Europe. Its arsenals, weapons depots, and trained officer corps did not disappear when Yugoslavia dissolved. When international pressure compelled the JNA to formally withdraw from Bosnia in May 1992, the Bosnian Serb leadership established the Army of Republika Srpska (VRS) on 12 May, absorbing the bulk of JNA personnel, heavy weapons, and institutional infrastructure stationed on Bosnian territory. This was not a nominal transfer on paper — it was the wholesale inheritance of a modern military’s equipment and command structure by one party to the conflict.

The Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by contrast, began the war with severe material shortages. When Bosnian Serb forces and remaining JNA units initiated military operations across Bosnia in the spring of 1992, the Bosnian government scrambled to arm its defenders from whatever sources it could find. The ICTY Trial Judgment in the Hadžihasanović case (IT-01-47-T) provides background findings on the extraordinary difficulties ARBiH commanders faced in forming, equipping, and supplying their units during this period. Soldiers frequently shared weapons, rotated rifles among positions, and improvised with hunting firearms entirely unsuited for organized defense.

The embargo was not hermetically sealed. Illicit arms transfers reached various parties through clandestine channels throughout the conflict, and in 1992, international enforcement mechanisms remained limited — there was no robust naval interdiction operation in place during the war’s first year. Yet these covert flows could not compensate for the structural asymmetry at the conflict’s foundation. The Bosnian government, internationally recognized as a sovereign state, found itself legally prohibited from acquiring the means of self-defense, while its principal adversary had inherited one of Europe’s larger conventional arsenals virtually intact.

This situation created agonizing choices for Bosnian political and military leadership. Some officials sought to circumvent the embargo through third-party networks, generating significant legal and diplomatic controversy. Others appealed repeatedly to the international community to lift or amend the embargo, arguing that its equal application to unequal parties produced deeply unequal outcomes. Those arguments found sympathy in Washington and other capitals but faced consistent resistance at the Security Council.

The arms embargo thus became one of the defining strategic constraints of the Bosnian War. Its asymmetric consequences shaped why certain positions fell, why certain offensives succeeded, and why the gap between military capabilities determined the war’s geography for years.

essays.title: Storming the Barracks: How Sarajevo Armed Itself
sources: ICTY Galic Trial Judgment (IT-98-29-T), siege context
essays.content:
When the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia entered its final dissolution in 1991, the question of who would inherit its military hardware became one of the most consequential disputes of the emerging conflict. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, that question was answered partly through a series of bold and chaotic operations from late April through May 1992, when nascent Bosnian government forces moved against Yugoslav People's Army (JNA) barracks and installations across Sarajevo. These actions, collectively known as the Battle of the Barracks, shaped the military balance of the war's opening months in ways that neither side had fully anticipated.

The immediate backdrop was the formal declaration of Bosnian independence in April 1992 and the simultaneous withdrawal of the JNA from the republic's nominal command structure. As the JNA began reorganizing its assets to support the newly forming Army of Republika Srpska (VRS), Bosnian Territorial Defence units and newly organized government forces recognized a narrow window of opportunity. Warehouses, depots, and garrisons inside Sarajevo held weapons, ammunition, vehicles, and communications equipment that could determine whether the city survived the encirclement rapidly forming around it. By early May 1992, Sarajevo was already facing a siege posture from VRS forces positioned in the surrounding hills, making internal resource acquisition not merely advantageous but arguably essential to the city's viability as a defensive entity. The broader context of the siege and its devastating impact on Sarajevo's civilian population would later be examined extensively in the ICTY Galic case (IT-98-29-T), though that judgment focused primarily on the sustained campaign of sniping and shelling rather than the specific barracks operations of spring 1992.

Bosnian forces engaged JNA installations at several locations, including the Marsal Tito Barracks and the Viktor Bubanj barracks complex. Negotiations ran parallel to confrontations, with some JNA commanders seeking safe corridors to withdraw personnel and equipment toward Serbia or Republika Srpska-controlled territory. These negotiations were tense and produced uneven results. The most documented and legally contested incident occurred on May 3, 1992, along Dobrovoljacka Street, when Bosnian forces intercepted a withdrawing JNA column. Bosnian authorities maintained that the column was being disarmed to prevent weapons from reinforcing the encircling enemy. Serbian sources characterized the incident as an ambush that violated negotiated safe passage guarantees, resulting in JNA casualties. The Dobrovoljacka Street events generated lasting legal and political dispute, with criminal proceedings initiated and contested for decades afterward.

Command authority on the Bosnian government side was fragmented during this period, with regular forces, police units, and independent armed groups sometimes acting without unified coordination. This complicated both the conduct of operations and subsequent efforts to establish clear accountability.

The practical consequences were significant. Bosnian government forces acquired artillery pieces, small arms, and armored vehicles that would sustain the defense of Sarajevo through the early months of the siege. Yet the weapons captured were insufficient to overcome the fundamental asymmetry facing the city's defenders against well-positioned and better-supplied VRS formations. The Battle of the Barracks thus represents neither a decisive victory nor a missed opportunity, but a foundational episode in understanding how Sarajevo's defenders assembled the means to resist during one of modern Europe's longest urban sieges.

essays.title: The Tuzla Column: Ambush, Seizure, and the Birth of 2nd Corps
sources: ICTY Mladic Trial Judgment (IT-09-92-T), JNA withdrawal and VRS formation context
essays.content:
In the spring of 1992, as the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia fractured along ethnic and political lines, the question of who would control the Yugoslav People's Army's (JNA) considerable arsenal became one of the most consequential strategic questions of the emerging Bosnian War. Nowhere was this question resolved more dramatically than in Tuzla, a northeastern Bosnian industrial city whose notably multiethnic civic identity had long distinguished it from the increasingly polarized politics consuming much of the republic.

Following Bosnia-Herzegovina's declaration of independence in March 1992 and its international recognition in April, JNA forces throughout the republic faced an uncertain future. Under international pressure and internal reorganization, the JNA began withdrawing personnel and equipment toward the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, while simultaneously transferring substantial assets to the newly forming Army of Republika Srpska (VRS). Bosnian authorities and emerging Territorial Defense forces watched these movements with acute concern, recognizing that allowing large quantities of weapons, vehicles, and ammunition to consolidate under hostile command would prove catastrophic for their defensive capacity.

On May 15, 1992, a JNA column departed its garrison in Tuzla, attempting to withdraw through the city under negotiated arrangements. What followed became known as the Tuzla Column incident. As the column moved through the city's streets, Territorial Defense units and local forces intercepted it. The precise sequence of events remains a matter of serious historical dispute. Violence erupted, resulting in casualties on multiple sides, with JNA soldiers killed during the confrontation. Serbian accounts emphasized the attack as an ambush and a fundamental violation of negotiated withdrawal guarantees, a characterization with legitimate basis in the documented timeline of events. Bosnian accounts emphasized the broader strategic context in which weapons transfers were actively arming forces engaged in campaigns of ethnic cleansing elsewhere in Bosnia. The legal and moral arguments on both sides reflected the impossible conditions of institutional collapse, where negotiated agreements and existential military imperatives collided with lethal consequences.

The strategic consequences proved significant regardless of interpretation. Bosnian forces seized substantial quantities of weapons, vehicles, and equipment from the column. This materiel substantially contributed to the formal establishment of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina's 2nd Corps, headquartered in Tuzla, which became one of the more capable and well-equipped formations available to Bosnian government forces throughout the war. The 2nd Corps was formally established in August 1992, through a process that drew on multiple factors beyond the captured equipment, including Tuzla's existing Territorial Defense structures and the organizational efforts of local military and civilian leaders. The ICTY Mladic case (IT-09-92-T), which examined VRS formation and operations across northeastern Bosnia, provides broader context for understanding the military transformation underway on all sides during this period of JNA withdrawal and successor army creation.

Tuzla itself, partly due to this early acquisition of resources and partly due to its prewar tradition of multiethnic civic solidarity, managed to resist the patterns of ethnic partition that devastated other Bosnian cities. The Tuzla Column incident illustrates the brutal strategic logic of the war's opening weeks, when institutional collapse transformed every negotiated agreement into a potential tactical calculation, and where the outcomes of single days determined the military trajectories of entire regions for years afterward.

essays.title: The Zenica Seizure: Arming 3rd Corps from JNA Stores
sources: ICTY Hadzihasanovic Trial Judgment (IT-01-47-T), 3rd Corps formation
essays.content:
Zenica, an industrial city in the Bosna River valley of central Bosnia, would become the headquarters of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina’s 3rd Corps — one of the more capable formations fielded by the Bosnian government during the war. The origins of that capability trace directly to the spring of 1992, when local Territorial Defense structures moved to secure Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA) garrison facilities before their contents could be withdrawn or transferred to hostile forces.

Following Bosnia-Herzegovina’s declaration of independence — ratified by referendum on 1 March 1992 and internationally recognized on 6 April — the JNA’s position in the republic became untenable under international pressure. Formal orders were issued for JNA units to withdraw from Bosnian territory, yet the process of withdrawal created an enormous practical dilemma: what would happen to the weapons, ammunition, and equipment left behind in garrisons scattered across the country? For the nascent Bosnian government in Sarajevo, and for Bosnian Territorial Defense structures and emerging government forces organizing throughout central Bosnia, this represented both an urgent opportunity and a profound risk.

In Zenica, local Territorial Defense and emerging Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina formations moved to secure JNA garrison facilities and their contents before those assets could be removed or transferred elsewhere. The seizure of weapons stores in Zenica provided critical material support for what would formally become the 3rd Corps of the ARBiH. These early acquisitions of artillery pieces, infantry weapons, and logistical stores gave the fledgling corps a meaningful foundation from which to organize and equip its units — resources that would otherwise have been extraordinarily difficult to obtain given the international arms embargo imposed on all parties in the former Yugoslavia.

From the perspective of Bosnian government forces, the action was a defensive necessity. Bosnia had been recognized internationally as a sovereign state, yet found itself immediately surrounded by armed formations and facing the prospect of being left defenseless. Securing any available military equipment was understood as an act of survival, not aggression. The ICTY Hadžihasanović trial judgment (IT-01-47-T) provides important background findings on 3rd Corps formation and early organizational development during this period, reflecting the improvised and urgent nature of military institution-building in central Bosnia throughout 1992.

From the JNA’s perspective, and that of Serbian political leadership, the withdrawal process was already contested territory, with competing claims over who lawfully controlled military property in a republic whose legal status remained disputed in Belgrade. Some JNA commanders attempted to negotiate orderly handovers; others sought to remove or destroy equipment rather than leave it in the hands of Bosnian forces.

The Zenica seizure illustrates a pattern repeated across Bosnia in the spring and summer of 1992: the chaotic disintegration of a federal military establishment created localized power vacuums that all armed parties sought to fill. The outcome in central Bosnia strengthened Bosnian government defensive capacity considerably, enabling the 3rd Corps to eventually field a coherent fighting force capable of holding the Bosna valley corridor against offensives from multiple directions.

Strategically, Zenica’s early arming demonstrated how institutional collapse simultaneously generates vulnerability and opportunity — a dynamic that would define the war’s opening months across the entire region.

essays.title: Visoko Depot: A Small Victory on the Sarajevo Approaches
sources: ICTY Hadzihasanovic Trial Judgment (IT-01-47-T), 3rd Corps formation
essays.content:
In the spring of 1992, as the broader conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina descended into open warfare, control over military installations and their stockpiles became a matter of immediate strategic urgency. The town of Visoko, situated roughly thirty kilometers northwest of Sarajevo along the Bosna River valley, became one of many contested points where newly formed Bosnian defense units sought to secure weapons and equipment that would define their capacity to resist in the months ahead.

As Yugoslavia’s federal structures collapsed, the Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA) found itself in an increasingly untenable position across Bosnia. Its installations, depots, and garrisons were surrounded by a population largely hostile to continued federal military presence, while its own chain of command was fracturing along ethnic and political lines. For Bosnian Territorial Defense formations, these garrisons represented not merely symbolic targets but practical lifelines — warehouses containing the rifles, ammunition, and supplies that fledgling forces desperately needed.

The Visoko depot action, which took place in approximately April or May 1992 as part of the broader wave of JNA facility seizures across central Bosnia, followed this wider pattern. Territorial Defense units operating in the Visoko area, drawing on local organization and popular mobilization, moved to secure the depot facility as JNA withdrawal became imminent. The operation reflected the improvised character of Bosnian government forces in this early period — men and women acting with limited coordination but considerable local knowledge and motivation. Detailed records of the specific units involved, the commanding officers, and the precise quantities of equipment captured at Visoko are sparse in the available historical record, and much of what is known comes from the broader context of 3rd Corps organizational development rather than accounts of the Visoko action specifically.

The ICTY Hadžihasanović trial judgment (IT-01-47-T), which examined command responsibility within the ARBiH 3rd Corps, provides general context for how forces in central Bosnia acquired their initial equipment through seizures of JNA facilities during this period. The Visoko area fell within what would become the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility, and materiel obtained from depots like the one at Visoko contributed to the corps’ early operational capacity.

From the JNA perspective, organized withdrawal under pressure was itself a form of strategic management. Commanders faced the difficult calculus of protecting their personnel while negotiating or contesting handovers of equipment. In many cases across Bosnia, these negotiations broke down, leading to confrontations of varying intensity. The outcome at Visoko tilted in favor of the Bosnian defenders, who secured a portion of the stored materiel.

Strategically, the significance of Visoko extended beyond the depot itself. The town sat astride routes connecting Sarajevo to central Bosnia, meaning that whoever controlled Visoko and its surrounding valley influenced the flow of supplies and reinforcements between the besieged capital and government-held territory to the northwest. For the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina taking shape that spring, small successes like Visoko carried disproportionate weight — both materially and psychologically, in demonstrating that organized resistance was possible.

Visoko would remain within Bosnian government-controlled territory throughout the war, serving as a logistics and organizational node for forces operating along the Sarajevo corridor. What occurred at the depot in 1992 was modest in scale but emblematic of the broader struggle to establish the material and territorial foundations upon which a prolonged defense would eventually rest.

essays.title: The Siege Begins: Sarajevo Under the Guns
essays.content:
On April 6, 1992, the day the European Community formally recognized Bosnia-Herzegovina’s independence, gunfire erupted in Sarajevo that would mark the opening of what became one of the longest sieges of a capital city in modern warfare. The day before, tens of thousands of Sarajevans had marched for peace, only to be met by sniper fire from the Holiday Inn, where Bosnian Serb political figures were meeting. What followed was a campaign of encirclement and sustained military pressure lasting nearly four years, reshaping the conflict’s entire strategic character.

The roots of the siege lay in the deep political fractures of Yugoslavia’s dissolution. As Bosnia moved toward independence, the Bosnian Serb leadership, organized under the Serbian Democratic Party of Radovan Karadžić, rejected incorporation into a sovereign Bosnian state. The Army of Republika Srpska (VRS), inheriting substantial weaponry and personnel from the Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA), moved to secure the high ground surrounding Sarajevo — the slopes of Trebević, the Sarajevo-Romanija plateau, and the ridgelines to the south and east. From these elevated positions, the VRS established a cordon around the city, cutting off the predominantly Bosniak and mixed-population urban center in the valley below.

The strategic logic was straightforward: controlling Sarajevo, the capital and symbolic heart of Bosnia, would deliver enormous political leverage. The ICTY Galić Trial Judgment (IT-98-29-T) found that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, under the command of General Stanislav Galić, conducted a prolonged campaign of sniping and shelling directed against the civilian population. The tribunal determined that this campaign was designed to spread terror among civilians and compel political concessions, constituting grave violations of the laws and customs of war. The ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) further documented how political and military leadership at the highest levels of Republika Srpska were connected to the operations encircling Sarajevo, establishing the chain of intent from strategic directive to artillery battery.

For the city’s defenders, the military situation was desperate from the outset. The Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina (ARBiH) lacked the heavy weapons necessary to break the encirclement, and the city’s approximately 300,000 remaining residents faced severe shortages of food, water, electricity, and medicine. The UN Protection Force (UNPROFOR) established a presence and took control of the airport, but its mandate constrained it from breaking the siege. A narrow lifeline — the tunnel completed beneath the airport runway in 1993 — eventually provided an underground corridor for limited supplies and personnel movement, though it could never substitute for open supply routes.

The siege transformed Sarajevo into an international focal point. Images of a modern European city under sustained bombardment generated profound diplomatic pressure on Western governments, accelerating debates within NATO and the United Nations about intervention and the limits of peacekeeping mandates. Yet that pressure would take years to translate into decisive action.

The beginning of the siege represented not merely a military operation but a defining political moment: a contest over whether a multiethnic Bosnian capital and state could survive. The encirclement would endure until February 1996, following the Dayton Peace Agreement. Understanding how the siege began — its strategic architecture, its human cost, and its political stakes — remains essential to understanding the entire trajectory of the Bosnian War.

essays.title: The JNA Withdrawal: A Handover, Not a Retreat
essays.content:
When the Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA) formally withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina in May 1992, it presented the withdrawal to the international community as evidence of Belgrade’s disengagement from the escalating conflict. In practice, however, the withdrawal was one of the most consequential acts of institutional restructuring in the entire war — a carefully orchestrated transformation that left Bosnian Serb forces better armed and more organized than before.

The context begins with Bosnia’s declaration of independence in early 1992. As Yugoslavia fractured, the JNA — nominally the federal army of a disappearing state — found itself deeply entangled in Bosnian territory. International pressure, particularly following European Community and United States recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina in April 1992, demanded that Belgrade withdraw its forces. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (FRY), formally proclaimed on April 27, 1992, needed to signal it was not a direct party to the conflict.

The withdrawal, completed largely by the May 19, 1992 deadline, was designed to satisfy that requirement. But the ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) documents in considerable detail what actually occurred. Officers and soldiers who were Bosnian Serbs by origin were transferred out of JNA structures and into the newly formed Army of Republika Srpska (VRS), established on May 12, 1992, under the command of General Ratko Mladić. Equipment — artillery, armored vehicles, ammunition stocks, and communications infrastructure — was left behind in quantities far exceeding what any genuine withdrawal would produce. The JNA did not strip the battlefield; it re-labeled it.

The continued relationship between Belgrade and the VRS following the formal withdrawal was a central issue in multiple ICTY proceedings. The trial of General Momčilo Perišić (IT-04-81-T), who served as Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav Army (VJ), examined personnel and logistical arrangements that sustained VRS operations well after May 1992. Though the ICTY Appeals Chamber ultimately acquitted Perišić in February 2013, overturning his trial conviction, the extensive trial record documented the institutional connections between the two armies — shared training pipelines, continued officer assignments across the nominal border, and material resupply channels. The organizational separation between the VJ and VRS was, in practice, more administrative than operational.

From a strategic perspective, the withdrawal transferred enormous military advantage to the Bosnian Serb leadership. The VRS inherited a disproportionate share of the JNA’s heavy weaponry in Bosnia, including tanks, artillery pieces, and armored personnel carriers. Bosnian government forces and Bosnian Croat units were left in comparatively weaker positions, with far less heavy equipment and no equivalent patron army from which to inherit materiel at scale. This imbalance would define the military dynamics of the war’s first two years.

For international observers and mediators, the withdrawal created a persistent analytical problem: it obscured the chain of command and responsibility. Belgrade could argue it had removed its army, while the VRS continued to prosecute operations with JNA-trained officers, JNA-origin equipment, and — as multiple ICTY proceedings established — ongoing material support from the FRY.

Understanding this event is essential for grasping the war’s early military imbalances. The restructuring of May 1992 was not a retreat from Bosnia — it was a reconstitution of force under a different flag, shaping the military landscape that all three parties would navigate for the duration of the conflict.
